cards.title: Creative Hit Rate: Measure Winning Ads Instead of Total Ads Launched
cards.summary: Define a creative hit rate as winning ads divided by total ads launched, and scale creative volume only when hit rate quality is maintained.
cards.use_when: Evaluating whether to increase ad production volume, or auditing why a high-volume creative testing program is underperforming.

cards.title: Avoid Flooding the Pixel With Low-Quality Creative That Creates Negative Events
cards.summary: Understand that Meta's pixel and delivery train on all traffic including non-converters, so unqualified clicks actively degrade targeting.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to bulk-upload thousands of AI/UGC ads, or diagnosing declining account performance despite rising spend.

cards.title: Avatar-and-Angle Framework for Top-of-Funnel Concepts
cards.summary: Turn one avatar's full list of problems into ad angles, then pair each angle with the avatar to form a top-of-funnel concept.
cards.use_when: Generating top-of-funnel ad concepts and creative briefs for a product, especially when stuck for angles.

cards.title: Mine Bottom-of-Funnel Objections by Calling Checkout Abandoners
cards.summary: Discover real purchase objections by phoning customers who abandoned checkout and by writing down objections you already know, then build one objection ad each.
cards.use_when: Building bottom-of-funnel retargeting creative or diagnosing why add-to-cart does not convert to purchase.

cards.title: Structure the Ad Account as Avatar/Angle 'Packs' Inside One CBO Campaign
cards.summary: Use a single CBO prospecting campaign with many ad sets ('packs'), each grouping ads by a single avatar and angle or funnel position.
cards.use_when: Setting up or restructuring a Meta ad account so you can read results and control spend by avatar, angle and funnel stage.

cards.title: Don't Do This If You Like This hook
cards.summary: Curiosity-plus-relatability hook format that opens short-form video with a forbidden-action premise tied to the viewer's existing desire.
cards.use_when: Writing the opening 1-3 seconds of a TikTok/Reels creative for a consumable or habit product (appetite suppressant, snack, supplement, beauty routine) where you need to stop the scroll before pitching.

cards.title: Problem/Solution comparison video with competitor callouts
cards.summary: Side-by-side demo that names specific competitor failures and demonstrates your product solving them in one continuous shot.
cards.use_when: Producing creative for a product in a category crowded with lookalike competitors (phone accessories, cleaning tools, kitchen gadgets) where buyers need a logical reason to switch.

cards.title: Transformation teaser: tease the result, don't reveal it
cards.summary: Curiosity-driven creative that withholds the end result and only hints at the transformation, using sound overlay and ingredient highlights.
cards.use_when: Creating branded creative for a results-based product (fitness drink, protein, skincare, body transformation) when you have no influencer and need a low-production asset for your own page.

cards.title: Reaction-style video: bottle the response on camera
cards.summary: Capture a real physical or emotional reaction to the product in one take and let that reaction carry the ad.
cards.use_when: Producing creative for products with a sensory or dramatic payoff — supplements, flavors, taste tests, nasal sticks, clothing transformations, before/afters.

cards.title: Misconception video: use a credible source to reframe a belief
cards.summary: Break down a common consumer myth with an authoritative voice, then position your product as the corrective action.
cards.use_when: Writing creative for a category with entrenched wrong beliefs or low awareness of the mechanism (sleep, breathing, skincare, nutrition) where you need to create demand for a solution buyers don't know exists.

cards.title: Comment-reply video: turn audience questions into creative
cards.summary: Film a direct reply to a high-engagement comment, demonstrating the product while answering the viewer's skepticism.
cards.use_when: Finding your next winning creative angle, or answering the objection that keeps appearing in your TikTok/ad comments (does it actually work, how does it stay on).

cards.title: Free tip / secret narrative that resolves into a product pitch
cards.summary: Tell a personal tip or 'secret strategy' story that feels like raw testimony, then reveal the product as the mechanism behind it.
cards.use_when: Writing creative for a supplement or consumable where buyers already live with a specific recurring annoyance (nighttime bathroom trips, poor sleep) and will watch a peer's story.

cards.title: Hook-Value-CTA structure for short-form direct response
cards.summary: The repeatable back-end structure the source applies across all reviewed formats: hook immediately, deliver value in the middle, pitch product and CTA at the end.
cards.use_when: Structuring any TikTok/Reels creative for a product, especially when adapting an existing winning format to a new product or angle.

cards.title: Bundle strategy to raise AOV when unit price is too low
cards.summary: Answer to low-margin unit pricing by selling multipacks rather than trying to raise the single-unit price.
cards.use_when: Pricing or merchandising a low-ticket product (the source's example is ~$4.99) where a single unit cannot carry ad spend, or when planning bundles for a consumable.

cards.title: Match creative format to product type
cards.summary: Selection guide mapping the source's seven video formats to the product characteristics that make each one work.
cards.use_when: Planning a creative testing slate for a new product launch or deciding which format to shoot first when budget or shoot time is limited.

cards.title: Don't Abandon Hook Testing Because of Andromeda
cards.summary: Andromeda may group near-identical ads but rotating substantially different hooks still unlocks net-new reach for fatigued winners, so hook testing remains high-value.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to keep testing hooks on a fatigued winning ad or to kill it and start entirely new creative concepts.

cards.title: Revive a Fatigued Hero Ad by Replacing Only the Hook
cards.summary: A proven testimonial ad that fatigued after months can be revitalized by attaching new 3-5 second hooks rather than discarding the asset.
cards.use_when: A previously top-performing video ad (e.g. testimonial) has fatigued after extended spend and stopped scaling.

cards.title: Four Levers for Varying a Hook: Angle, Offer, Avatar, Format
cards.summary: Rotate hooks along four distinct levers—angle, offer, avatar and format—to bypass Andromeda grouping and reach genuinely new audiences.
cards.use_when: Planning hook variations for a proven ad body and choosing which dimensions to change.

cards.title: Test More Than Three Hooks to Beat the Odds
cards.summary: Testing only two or three hook variations per concept has low odds of producing a winner; run many variations on a proven body instead.
cards.use_when: Choosing how many hook variations to produce when revitalizing a proven winning ad.

cards.title: Why Hooks Deserve the Budget: Drop-off Math
cards.summary: Most viewers drop off at the hook, so the first 3-5 seconds carry the highest ROI of the entire creative and justify disproportionate production effort.
cards.use_when: Allocating creative production time and budget between hooks versus full ad bodies.

cards.title: Distinguish EGC Hooks from CGC Bodies
cards.summary: Employee Generated Content (EGC) can deliver a new hook that leads into the original Customer Generated Content (CGC) testimonial body to re-hook audiences.
cards.use_when: Structuring a testimonial ad where the hook and testimonial come from different sources to expand reach.

cards.title: Raise the Quality Bar for Hook Variations
cards.summary: The mechanics of hook testing haven't fundamentally changed but the quality/requirement bar to make it succeed has risen, so weak or repurposed hooks should be expected to fail.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing why new hooks fail on a proven ad and deciding whether to blame the method or the execution.

cards.title: Frame-by-frame Meta video ad teardown workflow
cards.summary: A repeatable critique process for diagnosing why a video ad wins or loses before you spend more budget on it.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a live or draft Meta video ad for a product page traffic campaign and deciding whether to scale, iterate or kill it.

cards.title: Build hooks that select the right viewer
cards.summary: Strong hooks combine clarity, relevance, novelty, specificity and credibility to pull the correct target audience rather than indiscriminate attention.
cards.use_when: Writing or rewriting the opening 3 seconds of a Meta video ad for a cold audience where the previous hook had high views but poor conversion.

cards.title: Delay the product pitch: the bridge principle
cards.summary: Top ads transition from hook into education or problem agitation before naming the product, giving viewers a reason to keep watching.
cards.use_when: Scripting the 5 to 15 second section of a video ad where you currently introduce the product immediately after the hook.

cards.title: Turn features into lifestyle benefits (and lead with the benefit)
cards.summary: Every product feature in a script must be explicitly tied to a tangible lifestyle outcome, ideally by stating the benefit first.
cards.use_when: Rewriting a UGC or demo ad script that lists product specs without explaining why the buyer should care.

cards.title: Match the CTA intensity to the ad format
cards.summary: Soft CTAs suit educational scripts and partnership ads; hard CTAs jar when the rest of the ad is tonally soft.
cards.use_when: Writing the closing line of a video ad, especially a creator or partnership ad, where a hard sales close would break the format.

cards.title: Borrow authority from licensing and category history
cards.summary: Third-party brands, manufacturing origin and long-established design provenance can supply credibility at the top of an ad without founder fame.
cards.use_when: Selecting an angle for a cold-audience ad when your brand has no recognisable founder or following.

cards.title: Fix the attention-retention trade-off across hooks
cards.summary: Attention is not the goal; capturing the right viewer for the right reason is, otherwise retention and conversion suffer downstream.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing an ad with strong 3-second view rate but poor watch-through and poor landing-page conversion.

cards.title: Write scripts that do not depend on the founder
cards.summary: Ego-driven founder ads can convert on existing trust but cannot scale, and collapse if the founder's reputation is damaged.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to run a personal-brand-led creative as a cold-audience paid ad versus keeping it organic.

cards.title: Audit the click-through destination for live ads
cards.summary: Creative quality is wasted if the ad links to a broken or missing page; verify destination pages for every running ad.
cards.use_when: Running any new or inherited paid social account and checking where active ads actually send traffic.

cards.title: Use a numbered-reasons structure with wide pillar benefits
cards.summary: Numbered lists ('three reasons why') keep the ad scannable, but the pillars must be broad enough to reach a large audience.
cards.use_when: Structuring the body of a video ad for a consumable or routine product where you want a simple repeatable frame.

cards.title: Reposition the product against the buyer's self-image objection
cards.summary: Objection handling works best when the script explicitly calls out the identity or aesthetic barrier stopping a purchase.
cards.use_when: Selling a product category whose buyers reject it because of an image or identity association (for example, ergonomic chairs and the 'gamer' look).

cards.title: Recognise the structural signature of ads that burn money
cards.summary: The bad ads share the same failure pattern: no real hook, product introduced immediately, hard selling, no education or problem agitation.
cards.use_when: Auditing a new batch of ads before launch to filter out weak creative cheaply.

cards.title: Deconstruct Any Ad Into Messaging and Creative DNA
cards.summary: Break every paid social ad into seven messaging components plus the CAST video elements so you can diagnose why it works and clone it systematically.
cards.use_when: Auditing a competitor's winning ad or your own top performer to decide what to iterate on next for your store's creative pipeline.

cards.title: Build Audience Segments From Outcome × Demographic × Facet
cards.summary: Define granular ad segments by multiplying desired outcomes, demographic traits and specific facets, then write ads aimed at each slice for horizontal scaling.
cards.use_when: Expanding creative targeting for a supplements, health, skincare or similar store by finding untapped customer slices to write dedicated ads for.

cards.title: Separate Concept, Angle and Mechanism Before Writing Copy
cards.summary: Distinguish the core idea (concept), how you present it (angle), and why the product works (mechanism) so hooks and copy are built on clearly defined ideas.
cards.use_when: Planning the messaging layer of a new ad or landing page angle for a product whose core claim is still vague.

cards.title: Use the Six Copy Blocks as a Persuasion Checklist
cards.summary: Audit every ad and PDP against pain, promise, proof, curiosity, constraints and conditions — the Lego pieces of persuasive copy.
cards.use_when: Reviewing ad scripts or product page copy before launch to find which persuasion blocks are missing or weak.

cards.title: Write Hooks in Four Steps: Isolate, Commit, Deep Fry, Bang
cards.summary: Turn a basic product idea into a scroll-stopping hook by adding contrast, novelty and stakes, then emotional trigger words and open loops.
cards.use_when: Drafting the first 3 seconds of a video ad or the headline of a static ad for a new product angle.

cards.title: Pretend-Format Ads: Pick a Conceit That Fits the Offer
cards.summary: Choose the media format your ad pretends to be — interview, whistleblower, timeline, personification — and apply proven formats to winning concepts.
cards.use_when: Deciding the structural format for a new ad, or refreshing a winning concept that is fatiguing.

cards.title: Three Creative Types Across Three Funnel Stages
cards.summary: Classify creatives as branded, template or native, and place each at bottom-, middle- or top-of-funnel to keep the pipeline balanced.
cards.use_when: Auditing your ad account's creative mix to see whether every funnel stage has the right creative type for your store.

cards.title: Use the CAST System to Clone Winning Videos Element by Element
cards.summary: Break a winning video into Conceit, Actor, Style, Terrain and Setup, then rotate one element at a time to scale iterations efficiently.
cards.use_when: Producing multiple video ad variants from a single proven winner for a store without losing what made it work.

cards.title: Pattern-Detect Winners and Losers With Shared Grammar
cards.summary: Apply the messaging/CAST vocabulary consistently so you (or AI tools) can tag ads and surface which concepts, formats or styles actually trend.
cards.use_when: Reviewing account and competitor performance data to decide which creative elements to double down on for your store.

cards.title: Find Account Gaps With the Segment-Format Matrix
cards.summary: Identify creative whitespace by crossing possible segments with possible formats and styles, then flag which cells competitors cover and you don't.
cards.use_when: Planning the next month's creative testing calendar for a store and tired of producing variations on the same theme.

cards.title: STORMING: Diversify Idea Sources So You Never Run Out
cards.summary: Generate ad ideas from seven distinct sources — Swipes, Templates, Organic research, Matrix, Internal vectors, New styles, Gambit — to raise your hit rate.
cards.use_when: Filling a creative pipeline for frequent ad testing so ideas are not all rip-offs of the same competitor or your own brain.

cards.title: Make Strategic Bets: Cheap Iterations Usually Beat Net-New Ads
cards.summary: When choosing what to test with limited production and spend, prioritize rotating new conceits, facets, sub-outcomes or styles onto already-winning ideas.
cards.use_when: Deciding what to produce this week when editor capacity and testing budget are the real constraints for your store.

cards.title: Follow a Simple Production Workflow From Idea to Editor
cards.summary: Once the idea is chosen, write hooks first, use AI drafting with light manual edits on mechanism and copy blocks, then hand off to an editor with a winning reference.
cards.use_when: Running the day-to-day production process for paid social assets without overcomplicating the handoff.

cards.title: Run a Weekly Refinement Loop and Accept Most Ads Fail
cards.summary: Review your account, competitor accounts and the market multiple times per week, letting data sharpen your decisions while expecting most ads to underperform.
cards.use_when: Setting the operating rhythm for a store's paid social creative program so decisions get updated instead of set once.

cards.title: Develop Taste by Deliberately Practicing Ad Diagnosis
cards.summary: Treat intuition as a trainable, mechanical output of repeatedly analyzing ads and forming hypotheses, not a mystical gift.
cards.use_when: Leveling up your own or a team member's creative judgment so faster, better test-prioritization decisions get made for the store.

cards.title: Reduce Video Ads to Element Rotation for Efficient Iteration
cards.summary: Hold the winning element constant and deliberately vary exactly one other element per test to learn what actually drives performance.
cards.use_when: Scaling a proven video ad into a batch of variants for a store without wasting editor time on unfocused changes.

cards.title: Diagnose an Ad by Mapping It to Segment, Concept, Angle and Mechanism
cards.summary: Use a worked breakdown of a real ad to check whether your own creative clearly names who it targets and what idea and mechanism it carries.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a draft ad or existing top performer for a store to see if the underlying idea is strong enough before scaling spend.

cards.title: Write Ad and Landing Copy at a Third-Grade Reading Level
cards.summary: Keep storefront and ad copy at roughly a third-grade reading level so the maximum share of buyers reads it without friction.
cards.use_when: Writing PDP copy, product descriptions, ad primary text, email subject lines or landing page headlines where fast comprehension across a broad audience matters.

cards.title: Use Three Copy Frameworks: CJN, PAS and HSO
cards.summary: Choose among Challenge/Justify/Need, Problem/Agitate/Solution and Hook/Story/Offer depending on the audience's awareness and the asset type.
cards.use_when: Choosing the structural skeleton for an ad, email, PDP block, landing page or VSL before writing a single line.

cards.title: Give the Product a Unique Mechanism to Escape Commodity Comparison
cards.summary: Name and highlight the differentiated feature (the V12 engine) so the product escapes being compared on price as a generic commodity.
cards.use_when: Pricing or positioning a product that buyers treat as interchangeable; writing the differentiation block of a PDP or ad.

cards.title: Structure a Video Sales Letter and Landing Page Block
cards.summary: Map VSL and landing page architecture in a fixed sequence from audience call-out to risk-reversed close.
cards.use_when: Building a VSL script, a video ad or the text blocks of a landing page around a hero product or offer.

cards.title: Write Bite-Sized Email Copy First (200–300 Words)
cards.summary: Start with short email-sized copy because it is quick to finish, easy to critique and low-risk for beginners.
cards.use_when: Producing email campaign copy for a store, welcome flows, launch announcements or replenishment reminders, especially when developing copy skills.

cards.title: Run the Compile-Ideate-Structure-Polish Email Process
cards.summary: Use a repeatable four-stage process and timebox to write email copy consistently instead of from a blank page.
cards.use_when: Producing any email campaign for a store where you have source material (product details, founder video, past messages).

cards.title: Turn Creator Content into Store Copy with Transcript Distillation
cards.summary: Use video transcripts fed to AI to extract a brand's own language, hooks and stories for reuse in copy.
cards.use_when: Writing copy for a founder-led brand or creator store where you need the brand's authentic voice for ads, emails or PDP copy.

cards.title: Capture Hooks, Stories and Belief Shifts from Source Content
cards.summary: Compile a creator's own hooks, stories and belief-shift narratives so copy carries their voice and identification.
cards.use_when: Building an ad or email angle for a store where the owner has existing content (podcasts, videos, lives).

cards.title: Improve a Funnel by Improving Copy at Each Stage
cards.summary: Model the funnel as a chain (content → signup → open → buy → high-ticket) and improve the copy at every stage, not just at the buy step.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing where a store's funnel leaks — landing page signups, email opens, add-to-cart, checkout or upsell — and deciding which copy to fix first.

cards.title: Use Email as a High-ROI Channel for Store Acquisition and Retention
cards.summary: Prioritize email because the source cites it as the highest-ROI marketing channel and a 40x-better acquisition tool than social alone.
cards.use_when: Deciding which channel to invest store copy effort in for acquisition, re-engagement or cart recovery.

cards.title: Model a Launch Funnel with Copy at Each Stage (Alex Hormozi Example)
cards.summary: Use the source's worked example of a book launch funnel to see how better copy compounds through every stage to the high-ticket offer.
cards.use_when: Planning a product launch, pre-order campaign, live event or high-ticket offer funnel and deciding where copy improvements pay off most.

cards.title: Staff Copy Like an Owner: Buy Back Time with Reliable Copy
cards.summary: Small business owners outsource copy because their time is better spent elsewhere and poor work damages the brand more than it saves.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to write store copy in-house, outsource cheaply or hire a paid copywriter.

cards.title: Mine competitor video transcripts with an LLM for ad angles
cards.summary: Feed a proven creator's video transcripts into an LLM and prompt it for angles, stories, common phrases and audience-relatability hooks to speed up copy research.
cards.use_when: You need ad angles, email hooks or landing-page copy for a product in an unfamiliar category and want to absorb a proven creator's messaging before writing.

cards.title: Segment subscribers by how they joined before emailing them
cards.summary: Segment email subscribers by acquisition source—newsletter opt-in, free lead magnet, or past buyer—because each group expects different content and offers.
cards.use_when: You are planning an email sequence, welcome flow or promotion for a store and need to decide which message each segment receives.

cards.title: Build a prospect profile document from a brand's own content
cards.summary: Compile a creator's or brand's captions, hooks, sayings, angles, offer and stories into one document so your ad, email and PDP copy matches their voice and logic.
cards.use_when: You are writing ads, emails or landing pages for a brand or creator whose voice and offer you need to absorb quickly.

cards.title: Write a first marketing email as a story with a delayed reveal
cards.summary: Structure a promo email by stating the problem, hinting at the solution, deepening the pain, describing your own experience, then revealing the product and giving one CTA.
cards.use_when: You need to write a promotional email that moves readers from problem awareness to a click without sounding like an ad.

cards.title: Show your own conviction instead of telling readers they should buy
cards.summary: Persuasion friction drops when you demonstrate your own conviction and reasoning rather than repeatedly telling people they should buy.
cards.use_when: You are writing ad copy, emails or a sales page and catch yourself using pressure language like 'you need to get in before it's too late.'

cards.title: Score every asset against the four-part copy formula
cards.summary: Every piece of copy—email, ad, sales page—needs attention, consumption, persuasion and action, and the beginning deserves the most effort.
cards.use_when: You are drafting, reviewing or diagnosing any ad, email, landing page or VSL and need a checklist for what might be missing.

cards.title: Make a promise, not spam: lower reading effort and raise intrigue
cards.summary: Grab attention by decreasing the effort required to read while increasing intrigue; promises must be exciting but not spammy or platform-noncompliant.
cards.use_when: You are writing ad hooks, email subject lines or landing-page headlines and need to be exciting without triggering spam filters or ad rejections.

cards.title: Use the three-part attention formula: promise, intrigue, emotion
cards.summary: Grab reader attention by combining a non-spammy promise, non-confusing intrigue and emotional drama with a real payoff instead of clickbait.
cards.use_when: You are crafting hooks for social ads, email subject lines or opening paragraphs and need them to stop the scroll.

cards.title: Write for short attention spans by maximizing value per minute
cards.summary: Value value-per-minute over total value, using short sentences, bullets, visuals and a direct CTA.
cards.use_when: You are writing emails, PDP copy, ad creative or landing pages for an audience that scrolls short-form content.

cards.title: Vary pacing like an action movie to hold attention
cards.summary: Alternate slow, explanatory passages with short, fast, exciting lines so copy has natural rhythm instead of being all slow or all fast.
cards.use_when: You are editing an email, sales page or VSL script that feels flat, chunky or exhausting to read.

cards.title: Shift limiting beliefs before pitching the offer
cards.summary: People already know what to do; their limiting beliefs stop them—prove you understand the belief, disprove it, install the new belief, then sell using it.
cards.use_when: You are writing a sales page, VSL or email and the audience resists buying despite knowing the general solution exists.

cards.title: Submit evidence strong enough that belief follows
cards.summary: You cannot force belief by demanding it; supply evidence strong enough that holding the belief becomes difficult, using analogies, quotes, statistics, cost narration, hypotheticals and borrowed authority.
cards.use_when: You are writing a sales page, VSL or ad that asks the reader to change how they see a product category or accept a claim they may doubt.

cards.title: Specificity and Word Economy in Subject Lines and Email Leads
cards.summary: Cut ambiguity, front-load the hook and keep leads short so shoppers understand the claim in one pass.
cards.use_when: Writing or editing the subject line and opening lines of a promo or lifecycle email for a store, or A/B testing subject hooks.

cards.title: Cut Fillers, Redundancies and Vague Verbs From Promo Copy
cards.summary: Trimming filler, repeated ideas and imprecise verbs is one of the fastest improvements to any store email, PDP or ad.
cards.use_when: Editing promotional emails, PDP copy or ad copy before publishing, including cleaning up AI-drafted copy.

cards.title: Proof Elements That Make Product Claims Believable
cards.summary: Five proof types — statistics, cost narration, hypothetical examples, borrowed authority and analogies — support a claim before the buy click.
cards.use_when: Writing a product page, ad or email where a claim (better results, faster shipping, superior ingredients) needs supporting evidence before asking for the purchase.

cards.title: One Idea, One Action: Structuring a Single Promo Email
cards.summary: A per-email arc of problem, agitate, solution with one lesson and one clear CTA stops the reader being confused into inaction.
cards.use_when: Writing a single promotional or nurture email for a store where you need a clear arc from hook to CTA without overloading the reader.

cards.title: The Three-Pillars Offer Framework for Product Positioning
cards.summary: A reusable offer structure: what most people teach → why it's inferior → what you do differently → three pillars, with analogy and justification.
cards.use_when: Writing a sales page, video script or high-converting email for a store's flagship product, and reverse-engineering competitors' pages.
